# Capitolo 11: The Excavation

## The Public Court

The door had a name, and the name had a date. The date was 1312. The name was legal, bureaucratic, and almost boring. It was the name of a state that had learned to file, to label, to arrange, and to wait. In 1312 the pattern became legal. It became names, charges, lists, inventories, and public scandals. This was the old law of patterns: secrecy protects them until they are arranged, and arrangement makes them available. Availability turns mystery into a target. The danger did not arrive as a sword. It arrived as law. It arrived as a chancellery, as a council, as a dossier, as a conservation number, and as a door in a late-spring city.

When the pattern became public, it did not become safe. It became a scandal, and scandal is the public form of danger. In 1312, the danger became a court. The court worked with documents, names, property, and reputation. It did not need to understand the smoke. It needed only to make the smoke public. Once public, the pattern became available to chancelleries, lawyers, archivists, collectors, and committees. The danger became legal. The danger became administrative. The danger became French.

In 1310 the method had already been demonstrated. In the square before Notre-Dame, men who had carried the line were forced to confess, then to recant, then to die. The crowd did not understand the line. It understood spectacle. The state understood property. The legal machinery made the pattern visible. Visibility made it vulnerable. The 1312 dissolution formalized the process. It made the pattern into a case, a case into a document, a document into a resource, and a resource into a target. This was the new door. The new door was not a door of war. It was a door of law.

This is what the 1312 papers showed. The papers did not prove a treasure. They proved something stranger and more frightening. They showed that a pattern could survive by becoming famous. The Council at Vienne and the chancellery of Clement V made the pattern public. The court transformed the sacred into law, law into property, property into resource, and resource into danger. The court did not destroy the line. It made it legible. It made it available to chancelleries, lawyers, archivists, and hunters. A pattern hidden is safe until it becomes known. Once it becomes known, it becomes visible, and visible patterns attract hands.

This was the lesson carried to France. France had the lawyers. France had the chancelleries. France had the conservation offices, the municipal archives, and the patience of archivists. The French archive did not guard the pattern by hiding it. It guarded the pattern by making it available. Availability was danger. Availability was exposure. Availability was the modern form of the 1312 danger.

The French archive had a conservation number. The conservation number had a folder. The folder had a label. The label had a botanical line. The botanical line was the line of acacia. The line of acacia was the line of smoke. The line of smoke was the line of the threshold. When the line became public, it became available. When it became available, it became a target. In 1312, when the pattern became public, the danger became a court. In the modern city, the danger became a committee. The court and the committee used the same weapon. The weapon was access.

Access turned mystery into evidence. Evidence became law. Law became property. Property became scandal. Scandal became danger. The scent of resin remained because the line survived. The scent escaped through the wall because the trap had a wall, and walls could be opened. The line had moved from Egypt to France. It had moved from the vaults beneath the Al-Aqsa to the conservation offices of Lyon. It had moved from the chancelleries of the Middle Ages to the archives of the modern city.

In 1312, when the pattern became public, the danger became a court. In the modern city, the danger became a committee. The court and the committee arranged the pattern. They made it available. They made it vulnerable. The trap had a door, and the door had a name. The name was administrative, archival, and French. The name was the name of a committee. The scent had already moved through the wall. The line had already reached the street. The line had already become a door.

The committee in Lyon had already translated the pattern into paperwork. It had learned what the fourteenth century had demonstrated when the court at Vienne made the Templars public. A pattern hidden is safe until it becomes available. Availability exposes it. Exposure invites scrutiny. In the modern archive, availability had become bureaucratic. It appeared as a conservation office, a municipal stamp, a botanical appendix, and a public file. The committee did not hide the line. It arranged the line. It made the line available to curators, committees, museums, and governments. Availability was the new form of danger.

In Lyon, the archive had become the new temple. The wall had been opened not by violence but by conservation. The scent survived inside the stone because conservation preserved the residue. The residue was botanical. The botanical line pointed to acacia, smoke, and threshold. The committee had published the line. Publication made the line available. Availability made the line vulnerable. In 1312, the papal court at Vienne had exposed the line as a legal object. The court listed the chapels, the objects, and the relics. Lists made the line public. Publicity made the line dangerous.

In the modern archive, the committee had made the line available in Lyon. It had arranged a dossier inside a municipal office. The dossier carried a conservation number, a botanical note, and a photograph of the wall fragment. The scent was still alive in the paper. The line was no longer Egyptian. It was French. The line was no longer sacred. It was administrative. In 1312, when the court made the line public, the public made it vulnerable. The vulnerability became danger. The new danger in Lyon was not violence. It was access. It was exposure. It was availability. The trap was public, and public things attract hands.

In the archive, the committee had chosen the safest place for the trap. A wall in Lyon had once been a boundary. The committee had turned it into a cabinet. The cabinet had a label. The label had a botanical line. The botanical line was the line of acacia. The acacia was smoke, resin, and threshold. The committee had not stolen the line. It had published the line. Publication made the line available. Availability made the line visible. Visibility made the line vulnerable. The new threat had a municipal face. It had a conservation number. It had a door.

The new threat was not hidden. It was arranged. In Lyon, the committee had made the line available to public institutions. It had used the vocabulary of heritage, conservation, exhibitions, and cultural policy. The old sacred line had become a legal object, then a scientific object, then an administrative object. In 1312, this process had produced scandal. The court had made the line public. The public had exposed it. In the modern archive, the committee had made it available again. The trap in Lyon was municipal, slow, and bureaucratic. Its scent was botanical, Egyptian, and public. The danger had already begun.

The committee in Lyon had completed the arrangement. It had arranged the files, the labels, the photographs, and the public exhibition. The line was no longer inside a chapel. It was inside a municipal office. The new danger was administrative. It had the face of a conservation committee, the voice of a municipal office, and the patience of archivists. It had made the line available, and availability had made the line target. In 1312, public court produced scandal. In Lyon, public archive produced danger. The trap had opened. The trap had opened with a conservation number, a botanical label, and a municipal door.

The new threat had already arrived in Lyon. It had a French face. It had a municipal name. It had a conservation office, a public committee, and a door that had begun to move. The line had been public in 1312. It had been scandal in a cathedral. It had become law in a chancellery. It had become danger. In Lyon it had become available. Availability was the new danger.
